Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Raj was a 41-year-old South Asian man working as a park ranger, a job he had loved for years, surrounded by nature yet often feeling trapped within his own mind. His days were filled with the rustle of leaves, the chirping of birds, and the occasional encounter with hikers, but deep within, he felt as if he were navigating a dense fog, one that clung to him ever since that fateful day. It had been five years since he was held captive during a routine patrol in a remote area. The memory of those harrowing hours was burned into his mind, a series of snapshot memories that replayed like an old reel. He could still picture the dimly lit room, the faces of his captors, and the suffocating fear that wrapped around him like a vice. Each moment was a vivid picture, yet when he thought back, he often felt as if he were recalling someone else's experience, emotionless and detached from the horror that had unfolded.

Since that day, Raj's world had become a series of carefully constructed barriers. He found himself avoiding discussions about military topics, which seemed to pop up unexpectedly at gatherings or even in casual conversations with colleagues. When someone mentioned a military operation or a veteran's story, the sound of their voices morphed into a chaotic swirl of anxiety, leaving him hyper-aware of his surroundings. He remembered the feeling of being watched, judged, and vulnerable, and it made him want to shrink back into the shadows. Even the sight of someone in uniform brought a wave of panic that he couldn't shake off. He had come to believe that authority figures, particularly those in military garb, could only bring him harm-a belief that intensified the more he tried to convince himself otherwise.

Raj's coping mechanisms had shifted into maladaptive strategies that made him feel momentarily safe. He began to restrict his eating, a way to exert control over at least one aspect of his life. Skipping meals gave him a false sense of power, a way to combat the helplessness he felt during captivity. But with this control came the gnawing realization that he was slipping further away from his friends and loved ones. He felt as if he had become a stranger, isolated and set apart from the world around him. His girlfriend often suggested dining out or cooking together, but Raj would find excuses to avoid these moments, fearing that the act of eating alongside others would somehow expose his vulnerabilities.

In his mind, revenge fantasies surfaced like unwelcome guests. He imagined confronting his captors, picturing scenarios where he could reclaim his sense of agency. What frightened him most was the darkness of those thoughts; they felt like a slippery slope, leading him further into isolation and despair. He wanted to believe that he was not that person, yet the fantasies offered a temporary escape from the humiliation that haunted him. He felt permanently marked by what had happened, convinced that others would judge him harshly if they knew the truth about his experience. The self-comparisons that ran through his mind only deepened his despair, as he often thought that someone else wouldn't have found themselves in such a situation-someone stronger, braver, or more capable.

As time went on, the effects of his trauma manifested in ways that disrupted his daily life. At work, unexpected movements-like a colleague stepping out from behind a tree or the sudden rustle of wildlife-would send him into a startle response, heart racing and body tense as if he were once again in danger. His colleagues noticed his distance and reluctance to engage, but Raj preferred to keep his head down, feeling safer when he went along with whatever others wanted. Pleasing them became a strategy to avoid conflict, a way to blend into the background and shield himself from the scrutiny he dreaded.

It was only after a particularly vivid flashback during a community event-a moment where he felt as if he were back in that dark room-that Raj realized he couldn't continue living this way. He had been surrounded by friends and fellow rangers, yet the laughter and chatter faded into the background as he fought to regain his composure, the physical pain from the memory resurfacing in his body. It became clear that he had to seek help, to confront the shadows that had taken up residence in his mind.

Now, sitting in the therapist's office, Raj felt a mix of fear and hope. He was terrified of finally unpacking the trauma, of facing the memories that had haunted him for so long. But there was also a flicker of hope-hope that perhaps he could reclaim the life he once knew and rebuild the connections he had lost. With a deep breath, he began to share his story, ready to take the first step toward healing.
